anomaly_def.Name: SQL Workload Logic Anomaly + Schema and Index Design Anomaly + Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly
anomaly_def.Description:
SQL Workload Logic Anomaly : Application-level SQL or transaction design forces the engine to touch far more data, rows, or time than business logic requires.
Schema and Index Design Anomaly : Physical table, index, or partition design is mis-aligned with access patterns, forcing inefficient access paths even for well-written queries.
Data Block and Index Integrity Anomaly : On-disk pages or index structures are internally corrupted or inconsistent with logical row contents, making access paths unreliable.

When all three root causes are present simultaneously, the database executes bloated or chatty SQL against ill-suited physical structures whose very pages or index chains may be corrupt. Operators observe extreme and erratic statement latencies, frequent plan oscillations from targeted index lookups to emergency full-table scans, sudden surges in I/O and lock contention, and intermittent wrong-result or duplicate-row anomalies. Slow-query logs fill with the same heavyweight statements; integrity-check utilities intermittently flag corruption; index rebuilds or ANALYZE operations run longer yet fail to stabilize performance; application retries increase, and replication or backup processes report checksum or page-verification errors.

Causally, inefficient SQL magnifies row counts and touch patterns, stressing the deficient schema and overworked indexes; the absence or misconfiguration of covering and selective indexes further pushes the optimizer toward full scans that traverse broader swaths of storage. These heavier scans repeatedly hit corrupt pages or disordered index leaves, triggering error handling, plan fallbacks, or silent result inconsistencies. Conversely, corruption inside indexes can hide existing keys, making the optimizer believe selectivity is lower than reality, thereby reinforcing poor plan choices already induced by weak schema design and chatty SQL. The feedback loop—bad logic driving excessive access, bad design preventing efficient paths, and corruption breaking the remaining paths—culminates in a system where performance degradation, data inconsistency risks, and operational instability are all mutually amplified.

entry.official_definition: The length of time in seconds an InnoDB transaction waits for a row lock before giving up.
entry.trigger_condition: An InnoDB transaction waits longer than innodb_lock_wait_timeout for a row lock.
entry.workload_impact: The lock wait gives up; by default only the current statement is rolled back unless innodb_rollback_on_timeout is enabled.
entry.default_behavior: Defined as an InnoDB system variable.
entry.cause_analysis: This timeout is usually triggered when a statement cannot obtain the required lock within the configured waiting window because another transaction or metadata operation is holding an incompatible lock.
entry.solution_guidance: Inspect blocking sessions, reduce conflicting transaction overlap, shorten transaction lifetime, and review lock scheduling and schema-change timing.
